claims.text: Integrating machine learning with high-throughput experimental and simulation data will enable fine control of magnetic transitions and magnetocaloric effects in non-equiatomic HEAs.
Non-equiatomic HEAs have significant compositional disorder and complex local magnetic interactions.
First-principles calculations can supply finite-temperature magnetic information for an HEA.
High-throughput computational searches can efficiently explore HEA composition space.
A machine-learning model can integrate high-throughput experiments with DFT and Monte Carlo simulations to guide processing and composition adjustments.
Low-dimensional magnetocaloric operation occurs near critical magnetic transition temperatures.
Local atomic configurations critically influence magnetism near the transition temperature.
Processing produces local atomic configurations and microstructural features that mediate magnetic interactions.
The proposed framework can identify correlations among processing parameters, local compositional fluctuations, and electronic or magnetic structure.
Those correlations can predict shifts in magnetic transition temperatures.
Those correlations can predict enhancements in magnetocaloric response.
Machine-learning-optimized HEAs will have more finely tuned magnetic transition temperatures than samples produced using traditional compositional tuning.
Machine-learning-optimized HEAs will exhibit enhanced magnetocaloric effects relative to conventionally tuned samples.
Conventional methods relying solely on compositional adjustment provide less precise control over magnetic properties.
The degree of improvement depends on data quality, data coverage, and model robustness in a high-dimensional parameter space.
Magnetization-versus-temperature measurements can be used to determine magnetic transition temperatures.
Isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature change can be used to assess magnetocaloric performance.
